text: A swindler is handed a dead man's rank and told to wear it into a prison full of men who may believe him. The assignment is simple and foul. Be General Della Rovere, gather what the partisans say in the dark, pass it to the Gestapo. Rossellini made the film in 1959, a decade and a half after the occupation it stages, and Venice answered with a Golden Lion while the Academy gave its writing award. The interest is all in the mechanics of impersonation: borrowed authority, a salute returned a beat too warmly, a cell block turning into an audience that wants the performance to be real. Its 132 minutes are patient with that. What the con man puts at risk is not money but his working assumption that he is only ever playing himself.

Two cousins share an apartment in Paris, one of them there to read law and the other to throw the parties. Charles treats diligence as a method; Paul treats his own appetite the same way. Chabrol sets the arrangement up and then declines to correct it. Nothing rewards the studious cousin, nothing punishes the idle one, and Florence, who moves between them, is no one's prize to be won. Berlin gave it the Golden Bear. Study requires quiet, and the apartment supplies none. Almost all of the 112 minutes stay indoors, among young people who have made being amusing into a full-time occupation and are better at it than the newcomer will ever be. What the provincial boy stands to lose is not the girl but the belief he arrived with: that effort and outcome are related.

Berlin gave its Golden Bear to a film whose viewer average sits at 5.6 out of ten, and both numbers are reporting something real. Adina Pintilie built a project about intimacy and then placed herself inside it, following Laura, Tómas and Christian along a line between document and staging that she declines to mark for anyone watching. The demand it makes is not shock but duration: 125 minutes of steady attention to what people do with their fear of being touched, and to the spoken, awkward, adult negotiations that come before any of it. The European Film Awards named it the discovery of its year. A film assembled this way cannot be liked in the ordinary sense, and the split verdict on it may be the most accurate description anyone has managed.

Vic Brown cannot decide whether he wants Ingrid Rothwell, and while he is deciding, a pregnancy decides for him. That is the whole engine of this 1962 British film, which treats a young man's indecision as a serious matter rather than a comic one. Schlesinger keeps the story at work and in front rooms, in a country where the two of them will have to live inside other people's opinion of what they have done. The question is not whether they marry. It is the slower discovery that infatuation was never a plan, that Vic expected a life to arrive and has instead been assigned one, and that Ingrid has her own account of all this, in which she is not a consequence of him. Berlin gave it the Golden Bear, and it earns that in the domestic scenes rather than the romantic ones.

Any man who wants to marry Tuya must take her first husband too. She sets the condition without apology: a physical setback has made the household's work impossible for her alone, and her disabled husband is not up for negotiation. Wang Quan'an films the courtship as a practical matter: who can do the labour, who can be provided for, what a marriage is for when it has to function before it can mean anything. The suitors arrive less as romantic prospects than as applicants. Ninety-six minutes is brief for a story with this much country in it, and the compression presses everything into the space between one task and the next. Berlin's Golden Bear went to it in 2006. What steadies the film is Tuya, who refuses to treat her own arrangement as a misfortune while nearly everyone around her insists that it is one.

The shop is the point: Nathalie wants a boutique overseas and has no money at all. So a plan is made, and it is not complicated. She meets men with something worth taking, accepts an invitation home, and Eric and Bruno come in behind her. Nathalie is the bait and also the one who devised the scheme, which the film never lets slide out of view. Two of the young performers took César revelation prizes, which fits, because Tavernier is precise about how young the three of them are and how little thought any of this required. Berlin gave it the Golden Bear in 1995. What the 117 minutes keep measuring is the distance between a fantasy of a shop abroad and the physical acts required to pay for it, and how short that distance is for people who have never once had to test it.

She comes home to settle the family's business and finds the family's version of her childhood still in place, unrevised. Visconti gives that a hundred minutes and the shape of a mystery, though the crime, if there is one, is domestic: the questions concern what was done years ago and who agreed to say nothing, and every interested party is a relative. Venice answered with a Golden Lion in 1965. Sandra is an intruder in her own house, an adult standing in rooms that were organised around a child, asking for documents and being handed memory instead. Secrets here are not puzzles to be solved; they are the terms on which a household has agreed to keep functioning. What the film tests is how much of that arrangement survives one person's return.

Rehabilitation, in this case, means sorting scrap in a junkyard, and the film made about it is a comedy. The people assigned there have been classified as bourgeois by a state confident that useful labour will correct them, and among them a young man is courting a woman serving a sentence, which makes it a romance as well. Nobody in the yard is being asked to work so much as to be improved, and improvement is slow. Jiří Menzel keeps to 94 minutes and to a tone that never raises its voice; the jokes come out of the distance between the official purpose of the place and the entirely ordinary wants of the people standing in it. Berlin gave it the Golden Bear. What is at stake is not survival but frivolity — the right to want someone, to say something useless, to walk out of a correction programme uncorrected.

Rome's ring road closes on itself, and Gianfranco Rosi spent more than two years driving it in a minivan with a camera. What came back is not an argument about the city: a nobleman from Piemonte sharing a one-room flat with his student daughter, other figures who surface and are gone before anyone explains them, ninety-three minutes along a road built to arrive nowhere. Rosi had already filmed boatmen in Varanasi, dropouts in the American desert, killers in the Mexican drug trade; this time the unfamiliar country was his own. Venice gave it the Golden Lion, and the European Film Awards its documentary prize. The people living along the GRA are never converted into case studies, which asks a certain patience of anyone watching: nothing here is going to be summed up.

The residents of Wetherby are all very good at conversation, which is how the serious things stay unsaid. A young man nobody quite knows arrives in the suburb, and his presence works on that composure the way a stranger's question works at a table of old friends: what had been settled stops being settled. Mystery is the genre label, but the investigation runs into the residents rather than the event. David Hare directed, and the film is mostly talk, 102 minutes of fluency operating as concealment, the past pressing up underneath the present. Berlin gave it the Golden Bear in 1985. The suspense is not really about the newcomer. It concerns which of these self-possessed adults will break first and say the thing they have spent years not saying, and what it will cost the others to hear it.

In 1943, planes cross the sky over a Bengali village and nobody underneath has any use for the war they belong to. What reaches the village instead is hunger, arriving first as arithmetic — what food costs, who still has some, who can be refused. Satyajit Ray gives Gangacharan, the village's new Brahmin, a status that is purely social: he teaches, he performs the rites, he is deferred to, and deference holds its value only while there is food. His wife Ananga meets the same emergency differently, by feeding people, and the hundred and one minutes run along the gap between them. Berlin's Golden Bear went to it in 1973. Famine here is not spectacle; it is an administrative event, conducted in prices, favours and the order in which people stop being helped.

An American soldier goes home to the United States expecting a Polish woman and her mother to follow him. Everything in Krzysztof Zanussi's film lives in that gap, the interval between an agreement made in a wrecked country and the day it would have to be carried out. Norman and Emilia meet not long after the war ends, in conditions where housing is provisional and the right medicine has to be found before anything else can be arranged. Venice gave it the Golden Lion in 1984; the Golden Globes named it the year's best non-English-language film. A hundred and ten minutes, and they go to obligation rather than passion: what a daughter owes, what a sick woman is prepared to permit, and how little of a love affair here is allowed to be only that.

A rickshaw is a machine powered by one man's legs, and the man pulling this one owns nothing else. When a husband dies suddenly, he begins helping the widow and her son, and what grows out of it has no name: not adoption, not employment, not courtship, and never once discussed by the people inside it. Hiroshi Inagaki gives it 103 minutes and files it as drama and comedy both, with the comedy load-bearing, because warmth of that kind is what lets an outsider keep a place in a house he has no claim on. Venice gave it the Golden Lion in 1958. The tension is a matter of decorum — the boy needs him, the mother is grateful, and none of that settles what a man who pulls a cart is permitted to be to them.

Two stowaways are pulled out of a ship's hold and begin explaining themselves to the captain. She has been accused of collaborating with the Nazis; he is the freedom fighter who got her away from the reprisals, and Marseille, where this begins, has only just been liberated. Clouzot made the film in 1949, close enough to those events that the accusation was still a live matter rather than a historical subject. The 101 minutes are told backwards, to a man under no obligation to sympathise, which puts the pair in the position of arguing for themselves while the account of what they did accumulates. Venice gave it the Golden Lion. Their survival depends on a story they are telling out loud to a stranger who can hand them over at any point in it.
